newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US, angry with EU, expected to ignore WTO on Cuba.
newsitem.headline: US, angry with EU, expected to ignore WTO on Cuba.

text.p: The United States, furious with the European Union for bringing their dispute over Cuba to the World Trade Organisation, seems likely to refuse to cooperate with a WTO panel, diplomats said on Tuesday.

And trade envoys and business figures attending the Davos World Economic Forum and who had raised the controversial Helms-Burton law with U.S. officials at the gathering said they were struck by the bitter mood they encountered.

"There is no doubt in my mind that the U.S. will simply not participate in the work of the panel," said one envoy. "The Americans are very angry with Brussels for pushing the demand for a panel," a European company executive added.

The EU late on Monday formally asked WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero to create the panel by himself naming three experts to sit on it and study Helms-Burton to determine if it violates the global trade body's rules.

After the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body last November 20 authorised establishment of a panel, Brussels had appeared to hold back, while U.S. President Bill Clinton renewed a six-month waiver on a key section of the law.
U.S. officials had also delayed movement by rejecting earlier candidates for the panel put up by the WTO Secretariat.

Ruggiero, who had made clear he fervently hoped the two powers would make a deal and keep the politically- charged row out of the WTO's formal dispute settlement procedure, now has 10 days to appoint the panellists.
They would then have six months to come up with a finding, that could then be appealed by either side, extending the whole process well into 1998.
In normal circumstances, the two sides would make submissions to the three experts -- who will almost certainly be experienced trade diplomats -- and argue their case.

But the United States is insisting the law -- which formally aims to help restore "freedom and democracy" in Cuba by creating barriers to foreign investment -- is a national security issue, which puts it outside the WTO reach.

The EU, which has almost unanimous support among the WTO's 130 members for its opposition to Helms-Burton, argues that under the rules the panel itself will have to decide whether Washington is justified in pleading national security.
"In our view, the position is clear," said one U.S. source. "How can a panel of trade experts make a political judgement. Only a country itself can determine what affects its security."

Many trade diplomats and officials at the WTO's Geneva headquarters share Ruggiero's fear that the issue -- feeding on high emotions in the United States over Fidel Castro's Cuba -- could seriously damage the fledgling organisation.
They also suspect that the antagonism it is generating between the United States and the EU could rebound in other trade -- and even political -- areas where cooperation between them is vital.

Two senior U.S. figures in Davos -- Under-Secretary for International Trade Stuart Eizenstadt and Speaker of the House of Representatives Newt Gingrich -- spoke scathingly of the EU position and the "succour" it gave to Castro.

Only two weeks ago officials of the Clinton administration were hailing what they said was a shift by Brussels towards a greater emphasis on human rights in its dealings with Cuba, contrasting this with a "weaker" stance by Canada.

Some diplomats say the U.S. anger is also personal and directed at EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, never popular in Washington, who revealed from Davos that Brussels was pushing ahead with the case in the WTO.
